cues.text: Chapter two: blockchain and distributed ledgers.
Let us begin with the basic vocabulary.
A distributed ledger is a replicated record that is maintained across several participants, according to protocols they have agreed on.
So instead of one organisation holding the only copy, many parties hold copies, and rules decide how those copies are kept in step.
A blockchain is one particular way of building such a ledger.
It groups transactions into blocks, and each block is linked cryptographically to the block before it.
Two cryptographic ideas matter here.
First, a hash.
A hash is a fixed-length digest of some input.
The important property is that if you change the input, the digest changes with high probability.
That makes a hash a kind of fingerprint for data.
Second, digital signatures.
A digital signature authenticates that someone controls a particular signing key, and it protects integrity.
But notice the qualification: it does not necessarily prove real-world identity.
It proves control of a key, not who the person actually is.
Now look at the structure of the chain, shown in three blocks.
Block A holds its transactions and its own hash, called hash A.
Block B holds its transactions, plus the previous hash, which is hash A, and then its own hash, hash B.
Block C holds its transactions, plus the previous hash, which is hash B, and then its own hash, hash C.
So each block points back to the one before it by carrying that block's hash.
If someone altered Block A, hash A would change, and Block B's stored previous hash would no longer match.
That is how the linking makes tampering visible.
Next, how do participants agree on what is true?
Nodes verify the rules, and they use consensus to agree on the valid state of the ledger.
There are different consensus mechanisms.
Proof of Work uses computational work.
Proof of Stake uses stake-based participation, together with protocol incentives.
And permissioned Byzantine fault-tolerant approaches use known validators and voting.
The source is explicit that these are different mechanisms, not interchangeable guarantees.
You cannot assume that one gives you the same assurances as another.
There is also a distinction in who may take part.
Public permissionless ledgers allow broad participation.
Permissioned ledgers restrict participation, and for that reason can better suit inter-agency governance, where the parties are known organisations.
Now, smart contracts.
Smart contracts are programs executed according to ledger rules.
They automate conditions, so that when a stated condition is met, an action follows.
But they can contain defects, just like any program.
And when a contract depends on facts from outside the ledger, those facts need trustworthy oracles to supply them.
A word on immutability.
The source says it is better described as tamper resistance under protocol and governance assumptions.
In other words, the records are hard to alter, provided the protocol and governance hold.
Even so, a compromised key or a fraudulent original entry can still produce incorrect records.
The chain can faithfully preserve something that was wrong from the start.
And one more point: blockchains do not automatically encrypt data.
Being on a blockchain is not the same as being confidential.
Now let us compare a conventional distributed database with blockchain or distributed ledger technology, which we abbreviate as DLT.
The table has three columns: the feature, the conventional distributed database, and blockchain or DLT.
We go row by row.
First row, primary goal.
A conventional distributed database aims at scalable, coordinated data management.
Blockchain or DLT aims at a shared, verifiable history among parties.
Second row, control.
In a conventional database, control is often with one organisation or a trusted operator.
In blockchain or DLT, control sits with multiple participants under protocol and governance.
Third row, updates.
Conventional databases offer controlled insert, update and delete.
Blockchain or DLT is commonly append-oriented, meaning you mainly add new records rather than rewrite old ones.
Fourth row, performance.
Conventional databases often give high throughput and flexible queries.
For blockchain or DLT, the source says consensus and replication overhead varies, so the cost depends on the design.
Fifth row, use.
Conventional databases suit transactions and operational records.
Blockchain or DLT suits multi-party provenance and audit trails.
So when should you actually use DLT?
Only where independent parties need a shared, verifiable history and cannot efficiently rely on a trusted central operator.
If that condition is not met, the source notes that a conventional database with signed audit logs may suffice.
Finally, a caution about personal data.
Store sensitive personal data off-chain.
Even hashes or identifiers can be personal data, depending on linkability, that is, on whether they can be connected back to a person.
And because records are immutable, obligations around retention, erasure and correction are challenging.
If a person has the right to have data corrected or erased, an append-oriented, tamper-resistant ledger makes that hard to honour.
